|pages= |via=newspapers.com}}{{Rp|pp=18|page=}} In November 1937, ''Dione'' joined the search for survivors of the sunken cargo ship {{SS|Tzenny Chandris||2}}, which had sunk in a storm off [[Hatteras, North Carolina]], on the night of 12–13 November. Multiple lifeboats were found empty, but 15 survivors were eventually found clinging to wreckage by the cutter {{USCGC|Mendota|1928|2}} and were subsequently taken to Norfolk."[https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/sn83045462/1937-11-14/ed-1/seq-1/ Ships sweep sea for missing 22]". ''[[The Washington Star|The Sunday Star]]''. Washington, DC. 14 November 1937. Retrieved 7 March 2024 – via [[Library of Congress]].{{Rp|pp=|page=1}}{{Cite news |title=Freighter Leaky, Survivors Assert; Seaman Says Crew Asked That Ship be Turned Back Long Before She Sank |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1937/11/16/94460315.html?pageNumber=3 |access-date=2025-04-21 |work=The New York Times |language=en |issn=0362-4331}} === World War II === Following the beginning of [[World War II]],{{Efn|name=wwiiefn|group=lower-alpha|World War II began in September 1939, though the U.S. only entered in December 1941.}} ''Dione'' was assigned to both the [[United States naval districts#Fifth Naval District|Fifth Naval District]]—which contained the waters off [[Virginia]] and [[North Carolina]]{{Cite web |title=Torpedo Junction |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/wwii_caha_torpedo_junction.htm |access-date=February 7, 2025 |website=National Park Service |language=en}}{{Em dash}}and the [[Eastern Sea Frontier]], a Navy operational command. She was based out of [[Naval Station Norfolk#History|Naval Operating Base Norfolk]]. ''Dione'' was assigned to [[Maritime patrol|patrol duty]] of the waters between Norfolk and [[Morehead City, North Carolina]], covering the [[Sea lane|shipping lanes]] that passed by the [[Outer Banks]] of North Carolina and going as far out as the [[Gulf Stream]]. She also traveled to the [[lightship]]s that operated off the Outer Banks to deliver and receive [[mail]].{{Cite book |last=Hickam |first=Homer H. |author-link=Homer Hickam |url=https://archive.org/details/torpedojunctionu0000hick |title=Torpedo Junction: U-Boat War Off America's East Coast, 1942 |publisher=Naval Institute Press |year=1989 |isbn=9781612515786 |language=en |orig-date= |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}{{Rp|pp=|page=25}} On 1 November 1941, President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] signed [[Executive Order 8929]],{{Cite web |title=Executive Order 8929—Directing the Coast Guard to Operate as a Part of the Navy |url=https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-8929-directing-the-coast-guard-operate-part-the-navy |access-date=20 November 2025 |website=The American Presidency Project}} which transferred control of the Coast Guard from the Department of the Treasury to the Navy “for the duration of the emergency.”{{Cite web |last=Dropkin |first=Les |date=January 2002 |title=Sister Ships: The Thetis Class Coast Guard Patrol Boats |url=http://www.usspotomac.org/education/documents/sister_ships_coast_guard_patrol_boats.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101130203005/http://www.usspotomac.org/education/documents/sister_ships_coast_guard_patrol_boats.pdf |archive-date=30 November 2010 |access-date=21 October 2025 |website=USS Potomac |via=[[Wayback Machine]]}}{{Rp|pp=|page=16}} Sometime in 1941,{{Efn|name=rearmamentefn|group=lower-alpha}} the cutter's two {{Convert|1|lbs|kg|abbr=on}} guns were removed. Installed were two racks to hold [[depth charge]]s and a [[Y-gun|Y-gun depth charge launcher]], which was designed to throw depth charges over the sides of the cutter and into the water.{{Cite book |url=https://maritime.org/doc/destroyer/depthprojector1/index.php |title=Depth Charge Projector Mark I (or Y-Gun) |date=October 1918 |publisher=Government Printing Office |edition=Revised |pages= |language=en}}{{Rp|pp=|page=3}} ==== Second Happy Time ==== {{Further information|Second Happy Time|Torpedo Alley}} ===== January–⁠February ===== [[File:Fifth Naval District map.jpg|thumb|This map shows the [[Coast#Coastal waters|waters]] of the Fifth Naval District off North Carolina and Virginia which ''Dione'' patrolled during the Second Happy Time|alt=A map showing the shoreline of Virginia and North Carolina]] The waters off the Outer Banks of North Carolina are nicknamed the "[[Graveyard of the Atlantic]]" due to the high amount of ships lost at sea off the coast. The [[Shoal|sandbars]] shift due to rough waves and unpredictable weather.{{Rp|pp=|page=25}} During World War II, this region also earned the additional nickname "[[Torpedo Alley]]" (alternatively Torpedo Junction{{Cite news |last=James |first=Dale |date=7 October 1991 |title='Torpedo Junction' recalled at Dione reunion |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1185379651/ |access-date=22 November 2025 |work=[[The Huntsville Times]] |via=newspapers.com}}{{Rp|pp=|page=24}}) due to the high number of U-boats patrolling off the Outer Banks. During the time period that lasted from January to June 1942 and was referred to as the "[[Second Happy Time]]" by ''[[Kriegsmarine]]'' officers as well as [[Karl Dönitz]]—[[Admiral (Germany)|Admiral]] of the {{lang|de|Kriegsmarine}} and in charge of U-boats,{{Cite journal |last=Offley |first=Ed |date=February 2022 |title=The Drumbeat Mystery |url=https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/2022/february/drumbeat-mystery |journal=Naval History |publisher=U.S. Naval Institute |volume=36 |issue=1}} 397 [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] ships were sunk by U-boats. [[Adolphus Andrews]], the [[Rear admiral (United States)|rear admiral]]{{Cite web |date=10 April 2019 |title=Adolphus Andrews |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/research-guides/modern-biographical-files-ndl/modern-bios-a/andrews-adolphus.html |access-date=2 December 2025 |website=Naval History and Heritage Command}} in charge of the Eastern Sea Frontier, compiled a group of twenty ships to help defend the [[East Coast of the United States]]. This consisted of ''Dione'', six ''Active''-class patrol boats, four {{convert|110|ft|adj=on}} [[cruiser submarine]]s built before World War I, three [[Eagle-class patrol craft|''Eagle''-class subchasers]], two [[gunboat]]s from 1905, and four large [[yacht]]s that had been converted for military service.{{Cite book |last=Gannon |first=Michael |url=https://archive.org/details/operationdrumbea0000gann |title=Operation Drumbeat |publisher=Harper & Row |year=1990 |chapter=Waiting for Hardagen |access-date=21 November 2025 |via=Internet Archive}}{{Rp|pp=|page=176}}{{Cite book |last1=Blair |first1=Clay |author-link1= |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E8GDrZJEAGIC |title=Hitler's U-Boat War |last2=Blair Jr. |first2=Clay |author-link2=Clay Blair |date=21 July 2010 |publisher=Random House Publishing Group |isbn=9780307874375 |pages= |language=en |chapter= |via=Google Books}}{{Reference page|pages=461–462}} In addition to being the fastest vessel of the fleet,{{Rp|pp=|page=176}} ''Dione'' was the only one that was large and capable enough of opposing the U-boats that operated in Torpedo Alley.{{Rp|pp=|page=25}}{{Rp|pp=|page=102}} ''Dione'' was under the command of [[Lieutenant (navy)|Lieutenant]] Nelson McCormick at the start of the Second Happy Time in January 1942. McCormick came to the conclusion that ''Dione'' was too far away from ships, when they issued distress signals, to be able to assist them. Thus, he ordered his crew to conduct more aggressive and offensive patrols. After determining that U-boats generally attacked at night, McCormick decided to abandon his usual routine in favor of grid-searching the waters off the Outer Banks for U-boats;{{Rp|pp=|page=27}}{{Rp|pp=|page=28}} these would utilize a World War I-era [[sonar]] system{{Rp|pp=|page=24}} and other types of [[Sound recognition|sound-detection gear]].{{Rp|pp=|page=27}}{{Cite web |last1=Marx |first1=Deborah |last2=Delgado |first2=James |author-link2=James P. Delgado |date=April 26, 2013 |title=National Register of Historic Places Multiple Property Documentation Form |url=https://nmsmonitor.blob.core.windows.net/monitor-prod/media/docs/20130426-national-register-of-historic-places-multiple-property.pdf |access-date=April 21, 2025 |publisher=[[National Park Service]] |page= |via=}}{{Rp|pp=|page=28}}[[File:Dione_depth_charges.png|thumb|''Dione'' deploying depth charges, 1942|alt=Water is churned up behind the cutter as she moves forward]]Sometime at the end of January, ''Dione'' dropped six depth charges after her sonar operator reported an "underwater object" {{Convert|20|mi|km}} off [[Oregon Inlet]]. Two airplanes made several runs on a rapidly spreading patch of oil. They reported to McCormick that they saw something long and narrow. An oar and a boat hook eventually surfaced from the object, and when brought aboard were found to have been from the shipwreck of the [[oil tanker]] {{SS|Francis E. Powell||2}}; the tanker had been sunk by {{GS|U-130|1941|2}} on 27 January.{{Rp|pp=27–28|page=}} In early February, ''Dione'' was ordered to [[Joint Expeditionary Base–Little Creek#World War II|Little Creek Section Base]] to pick up a new master, Lieutenant James Alger. McCormick was kept aboard ''Dione'' as an executive officer, and to command the cutter when intricate maneuvers were required. On Alger's first day, ''Dione''{{'}}s sonar operator called out two echoes; the second resulted in Alger giving an order to drop depth charges. Two life rafts were dispatched to collect samples of oil that bubbled to the surface. It was then discovered that ''Dione'' had dropped depth charges on a sunken oil tanker.{{Rp|pp=28, 33|page=}} On 12 February, the cutter's sonar operator reported a [[periscope]] off ''Dione''{{'}}s [[Port and starboard|port side]]. Alger ordered [[general quarters]] and had depth charges dropped from both the Y-gun and the racks; some went off at {{Convert|100|ft|m}} while others went off at {{Convert|50|ft|m}}. ''Dione''{{'}}s lights and equipment abruptly went dead after her propellers came out of the water. The cutter's engines were stopped, and her electrical power was later restored. No U-boat was ever spotted.{{Rp|pp=|page=41}} {{Paragraph break}} Later that month, on 19 February, the cutter towed the [[minesweeper]] {{USS|Paramount}} to Morehead City after she had been grounded at the entrance to [[Ocracoke Inlet]].{{Rp|pp=|page=46}}{{Cite web |date=August 18, 2015 |title=Paramount |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/p/paramount.html |access-date=April 21, 2025 |website=Naval History and Heritage Command |language=en-US}} ''Dione'' set off for [[Cape Henry]] late at night on 27 February to assist the torpedoed [[Cargo ship|freighter]] ''North Sea''. The freighter was found by ''Dione'' early the next morning. Reportedly, a U-boat's attack on ''North Sea'' had been halted due to a storm that had tossed the U-boat about, preventing it from accurately aiming its [[deck gun]] and shelling the freighter. ''Dione'' towed the damaged freighter to [[Joint Expeditionary Base–Little Creek#World War II|Little Creek]], as ''North Sea'' had lost her steering capabilities in the attack, and arrived by the end of the day.{{Rp|pp=|page=50}} Sometime in February 1942, the ''Thetis'' class patrol boats were issued alpha-numeric designations, that began with WPC{{Rp|page=166}}{{Rp|pp=|page=18}}{{Em dash}}PC stood for [[Patrol boat|patrol craft]], and the W marked that it was part of the Coast Guard. ''Dione'' was issued the designation WPC-107.{{Rp|pp=|page=18}} ===== March–⁠April ===== [[File:Dione_rescue.png|thumb|''Dione'''s crew rescuing that of a torpedoed ship, 1942|alt=Crewmen peer over the side of Dione to pick up survivors of a shipwreck|left]] On 15 March, ''Dione'' received a distress signal from the oil tanker ''Australia''. The tanker had been torpedoed by {{GS|U-332||2}} about {{Convert|20|mi|km}} away from the cutter. ''Dione'' spotted ''Australia'' a little after an hour, and the cutter's sonar operator had picked up an echo from the U-boat within two. ''Dione'' launched depth charges but had no success.{{Cite book |last=Bunch |first=Jim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C4wtDwAAQBAJ |title=U-Boats Off the Outer Banks |date=10 July 2017 |publisher=[[History Press]] |isbn=9781439661734 |pages= |via=Google Books}}{{Rp|pp=79–80|page=}} ''Dione'' rescued the crew of the storage tanker [[USS Abarenda (IX-131)|''Acme'']] early in the morning of 18 March.{{Cite book |last=Cressman |first=Robert |url=https://archive.org/details/TheOfficialChronologyOfTheUSNavyInWorldWarII/ |title=The Official Chronology of the U.S. Navy in World War II |publisher=Naval Institute Press |year=2000 |language=en |access-date=21 November 2025 |via=Internet Archive}}{{Rp|page=170}} The tanker had been torpedoed by [[German submarine U-124 (1940)|''U-124'']] {{Convert|1|nmi|lk=in|spell=in}} west of the [[Diamond Shoals]] Light Buoy just before midnight the previous day.{{Cite web |last=Cressman |first=Robert J. |date=July 12, 2022 |title=Abarenda II (IX-131) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/a/abarenda-ix-131-ii.html |access-date=September 4, 2025 |website=Naval History and Heritage Command}} The cutter also picked up the survivors of the Greek freighter {{SS|Kassandra Louloudis||2}}, which had been torpedoed by the same U-boat that attacked ''Acme'' just after midnight on 18 March.{{Rp|page=170}} The cutter took the survivors of both ships to Norfolk.{{Cite web |title=Kassandra Louloudis |url=https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/kassandra.html |access-date=August 10, 2025 |website=Monitor National Marine Sanctuary}} On 20 March, ''Dione'' made contact with a U-boat. A Coast Guard airplane from the [[Coast Guard Air Station Elizabeth City|Elizabeth City Air Station]] dropped two depth charges. On 23 March, she responded to the distress signals of the oil tanker ''[[SS Naeco|Naeco]]'', torpedoed by ''U-124''. The cutter rescued at least ten survivors from a lifeboat and two more from the water, all of whom were taken to Norfolk.{{Rp|pp=96–98|page=}}{{Cite web |title=Naeco |url=https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/naeco.html |access-date=September 3, 2025 |website=Monitor National Marine Sanctuary}} Three days later, on 26 March, the crew of ''Dione'' spotted flames from the oil tanker {{SS|Dixie Arrow||2}} and traveled several miles to investigate. The tanker's survivors had already been rescued by the destroyer {{USS|Tarbell}}, and the cutter encountered nothing but debris. ''Dione'' then headed south to the waters off Hatteras, North Carolina.{{Rp|pp=|page=102}} On 5 April, the cutter responded to the torpedoed oil tanker {{SS|Byron D. Benson||2}}, and pulled one survivor from the water.{{Rp|pp=|page=123}} On 7 April, {{GS|U-552||2}} torpedoed the oil tanker {{MV|British Splendour||2}}.{{Cite web |title=British Splendour |url=https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/britishsplendour.html |access-date=22 November 2025 |website=Monitor National Marine Sanctuary}} ''Dione'' dropped depth charges on the U-boat which reportedly almost hit,{{Cite news |last=Levins |first=Harry |date=23 August 2003 |title=WWII veterans recall some trickery maneuvers against a ship's crew and a general |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/141018967/ |access-date=22 November 2025 |work=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]] |via=newspapers.com}}{{Rp|pp=|page=7}}{{Cite news |last=Levins |first=Harry |title=From Depths of World War, Foes No More |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/139690407/ |access-date=22 November 2025 |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |via=newspapers.com}}{{Rp|pp=|page=129}} though ''U-552'' managed to escape.{{Rp|pp=|page=129}}[[File:Dione escort.jpg|alt=An oil tanker is half-visible just behind the stern of Dione; the tanker is partially cut out by the camera's frame|thumb|''Dione'' escorting a convoy, 1942; her Y-gun can be seen behind the sailor in the foreground]] ''Dione'' rendezvoused with the destroyer {{USS|Dickerson}} on 14 April, near the Diamond Shoals Light Buoy, to escort a [[List of Allied convoys during World War II by region#North American coastal and Caribbean convoys|convoy]]. Lieutenant Dick Bacchus had taken over as the cutter's navigator and executive officer, arriving on 11 April from {{USCGC|Modoc}}; Alger remained aboard as the commander. The convoy was later joined by another cutter, and escorted two freighters north past North Carolina. After ''Dickerson'' relieved both cutters of duty, ''Dione'' headed back south for a nightly patrol. At morning on 15 April, the cutter met up with ''Dickerson'' once more to escort a convoy, this time consisting of two British trawlers, two American tankers, and an American freighter. The tankers were quicker than the cutter, and she had issues keeping up. Alger chose to be aggressive despite the fact that the cutter was supposed to remain close by the convoy, ranging out and dropping depth charges on any suspected echoes to "keep the U-boat[s] off balance."{{Rp|pp=164–166|page=}} For the next few days, ''Dione'' escorted convoys during the day and patrolled the waters for U-boats during the night. The convoys were nicknamed "[[bucket brigade]]s" after the old-fashioned method of transporting buckets during a fire.{{Rp|pp=|page=167}} These convoys traveled during the day and then docked in ports overnight; this was possible on the East Coast due to its abundance of good harbors.{{Cite book |last=Morison |first=Samuel Eliot |title=Volume I: The Battle of the Atlantic, September 1939 - May 1943 |publisher=Little, Brown and Co. |year=1947 |location=Boston}}{{Reference page|pages=132–133, 254–256}} No ships were lost to U-boats near [[Cape Hatteras]] or [[Cape Lookout (North Carolina)|Cape Lookout]] after the establishment of the "bucket brigade" convoy system.{{Rp|pp=|page=167}} On 18 April, ''Dione'' was observed dropping depth charges on a U-boat, with no visible results. On 19 April, ''Dione'' led a convoy of nine civilian vessels alongside another 88-foot cutter. The convoy passed Cape Hatteras without incident. A Navy aircraft spotted an incoming torpedo; Alger ordered evasive maneuvers. The torpedo missed ''Dione'' by about 20 yards but struck the oil tanker ''Axtell J. Byles'' at 2000 hours, which sank some time thereafter. ''Dione'' dropped eight depth charges over the course of two runs in response to the attack.{{Rp|pp=167–170|page=}} The convoys began to run at night following the loss of ''Axtell J. Byles''.{{Rp|pp=|page=178}} ''Dione'' began patrolling around the [[Wimble Shoals]] Buoy after her escort missions were finished, beginning demolition exercises on the wreck of ''Axtell J. Byles'' on April 25. She would continue dropping depth charges for the next few days.{{Rp|pp=|page=178}} On 29 April, ''Dione'' was ordered back to Little Creek for repairs and rearmament.{{Efn|name=rearmamentefn|group=lower-alpha}} ===== May–⁠June ===== The repairs to ''Dione'' were finished on 13 May.{{Rp|pp=178, 231|page=}} Leaving Little Creek, she was accompanied by a writer and [[Photojournalism|photographer]] from ''[[The Saturday Evening Post]]''. The cutter escorted two ships and afterwards dropped depth charges on an unknown sonar ping that the writer from ''The Saturday Evening Post'' had called "Wimble Willy."{{Rp|pp=231–232|page=}} The photographs were published in a 1942 article. [[File:Convoy in WWII off North Carolina.jpg|thumb|A convoy off the coast of North Carolina sometime during World War II. ''Dione'' escorted similar convoys during the latter half of the Second Happy Time]] On 18 May, ''Dione'' left Norfolk to join a convoy heading to [[Key West]], [[Florida]]. On 20 May, it was discovered that the cutter's port engine was "acting up". It was decided that she would continue on the convoy running on one engine while her other one was repaired. ''Dione'' traveled in the starboard quarter of the convoy and occasionally traveled further away from the convoy to listen for sonar pings. The cutter was eventually forced to fall to the rear position after a ship began lagging behind. The convoy reached Florida on 23 May.{{Rp|pp=233–235|page=}} Sometime in May, ''Dione'' met up with the destroyer {{USS|Ellis|DD-154|6}}. The two vessels completed support missions and responded to Coast Guard aircraft reports, steaming to the location of two allegedly damaged and submerged U-boats roughly {{Convert|50|mi|km}} off the coast of [[New Jersey]] and dropping depth charges on them.{{Rp|pp=|page=102}} On 15 June, a convoy ''Dione'' was escorting formed a single-file line in preparation to enter the [[Chesapeake Bay]]. The fifth oil tanker in line, ''Robert C. Tuttle'', struck a [[Naval mine|mine]] and began to sink within view of vacationers in [[Virginia Beach, Virginia|Virginia Beach]].{{Rp|pp=254–255|page=}} The oil tanker ''Esso Augusta'' broke the formation as her crew believed that ''Robert C. Tuttle'' had been torpedoed by a U-boat, and ''Esso Augusta'' ended up striking a second mine as a result. ''Dione'' dropped a spread of eight depth charges, and her ninth caused another explosion to occur. Eyewitnesses claimed to have seen a U-boat, but naval officials concluded that the incident was due to mines laid in the [[Thimble Shoal Channel]] between Virginia Beach and [[Eastern Shore of Virginia|Virginia's eastern shore]].{{Cite web |last=Offley |first=Ed |date=June 2022 |title=When War Erupted Off Virginia Beach |url=https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/2022/june/when-war-erupted-virginia-beach |access-date=May 12, 2025 |website=U.S. Naval Institute}} On 24 June, at 1900 hours, the cutter made an underwater contact while escorting a northbound convoy of eleven ships.{{Rp|pp=|page=607}} Five minutes later, ''Dione'' dropped one depth charge with no results. After sunset,{{Rp|pp=|page=607}} at 1910 hours, two other ships in the convoy, ''Nordland '' and ''Manuela'', were torpedoed by {{GS|U-404||2}}.{{Rp|pp=|page=607}} ''Dione'' made a sweeping search for the U-boat, which seemed to be on the starboard side of the convoy. ''Nordland'' caught fire and sink, and her survivors were rescued by ''Norwich City''. ''U-404'' attempted a second attack, but was stopped before it could do so by ''Dione'' and an aircraft.{{Rp|pp=|page=607}} ''Dione'' made an underwater contact the next day, 25 June, dropping five depth charges. Large amounts of oil bubbled to the surface. A doubtful contact was made just two days later, on 27 June, at 1054 hours. The cutter dropped four depth charges but yielded no results. ''Dione'' was taken to Norfolk for repairs to her starboard engine at the end of the month. They lasted a week, and the cutter was back into action at the beginning of July.{{Rp|pp=313, 321|page=}} She continued her convoy escort duties into July and August,{{Rp|pp=|page=322}} though the U-boat threat off the Outer Banks had become non-existent by then.{{Rp|pp=322–325|page=}} Following the [[Second Happy Time#US convoys arrive|end of the Second Happy Time]], the crew of ''Dione'' began to refer to the period as the "Battle of Torpedo Junction."{{Rp|pp=|page=19}} ==== September 1942–1944 ==== ''Dione'' was listed as a convoy escort unit{{Cite book|title=War Diary Eastern Sea Frontier; December 1943|publisher=Eastern Sea Frontier|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/78362039|via=[[National Archives Catalog]]|chapter=Appendix D. ⁠– Patrol Log|access-date=29 November 2025}}{{Rp|pp=|page=119}} and conducted escort duty in the [[Atlantic Ocean#North Atlantic|North Atlantic Ocean]],{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1206159471/?match=5&terms=%22cutter%20Dione%22|title='So Proudly We Hail' To Be New Column Feature|date=19 November 1943|access-date=30 November 2025|work=The Boonville Daily News|via=newspapers.com}}{{Rp|pp=|page=3}} escorting HK convoys going from New York to Key West{{Cite book|title=War Diary Eastern Sea Frontier; December 1944|publisher=Eastern Sea Frontier|chapter=Appendix G. – Patrol Log|via=National Archives Catalog|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/139752111?objectPage=3|access-date=29 November 2025}}{{Rp|pp=|page=122}} and KN convoys heading from Key West to New York. She was based out of [[Tompkinsville, Staten Island]] from December 1943{{Rp|pp=|page=49}} to December 1944;{{Cite book|title=War Diary Eastern Sea Frontier; November 1944|publisher=Eastern Sea Frontier|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/139832151|chapter=Appendix C. – Tables of Availability; 2. – Surface Craft|via=National Archives Catalog|access-date=29 November 2025}}{{Rp|pp=|page=53}} Thompkinsville was the site of an Eastern Sea Frontier Base.{{Cite web|url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/c/conemaugh-ii.html|title=Conemaugh II (AOG-62)|date=8 June 2022|access-date=29 November 2025|website=Naval History and Heritage Command|last=Cressman|first=Robert J.}} ==== 1945 ==== [[File:German_submarine_U-1228_surrenders_at_Portsmouth_NH_in_May_1945.jpg|thumb|''Dione'' (center) escorts ''U-1228'' to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on 17 May 1945|alt=A submarine is in the foreground; to its right are two ships. Dione is to the left, and a smaller unknown ship is to the right|left]] In 1945, ''Dione'' underwent a major refit. Her 3-inch/23-caliber gun was removed. In addition to her Y-gun and two depth charge racks, the cutter was fitted with two single-mount [[3-inch/50-caliber gun]]s, two single-mount [[Oerlikon 20 mm cannon|20 mm/80 cannons]], two [[Mousetrap (weapon)|"Mousetrap" anti-submarine rocket launchers]], and an additional Y-gun. Her wireless set and World War I-era sonar system was replaced with an SF [[radar]] system and a QCN-1 sonar system.{{Reference page|pages=37–38}} ''Dione'''s displacement was increased to {{convert|350|LT|t}} and her draft was increased to {{Convert|10|ft|m|0}}. Her complement was also increased to 7 officers and 68 men. The cutter was selected as one of six patrol vessels to serve as the Navy's "Surrender Group" for the [[United States naval districts#First Naval District|First Naval District]] off [[New England]], and served alongside her sister ships {{USCGC|Argo||2}} and ''Nemesis''. The role of the Surrender Group was to help escort surrendered [[Axis powers|Axis]] vessels to American ports, where they would then be acquired by the [[Federal government of the United States|United States government]]. Dönitz, now serving as [[President of Germany (1919–1945)|President of Germany]] following the death of [[Adolf Hitler]], had broadcast an order for all U-boats to surrender to Allied ports in early May.{{Cite journal |last=Thiesen |first=William H. |date=October 2016 |title=The Coast Guard's World War II Crucible |url=https://www.usni.org/magazines/naval-history-magazine/2016/october/coast-guards-world-war-ii-crucible |journal=Naval History |publisher=U.S. Naval Institute |volume=30 |issue=5 |access-date=August 25, 2025}}{{Cite journal |last=Theisen |first=William H. |date=Spring 2013 |title=Lieutenant Eliot Winslow, Kapitänleutnant Johann-Heinrich Fehler and the Surrender of the Nazis' Top-Secret Submarine, U-234 |url=https://issuu.com/seahistory/docs/sh_142_spring-2013 |journal=Sea History |issue=142 |pages= |via=issuu.com}}{{Reference page|pages=|page=18}} On 17 May, ''Dione'' rendezvoused with {{GS|U-1228||2}}, a U-boat that had fled to Allied waters following the German surrender. It had received its surrender orders on 9 May and was instructed to head to [[St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador|St. John's, Newfoundland]]. The U-boat bypassed St. John's due to poor conditions and headed to a new surrender point at [[Casco Bay]]. ''U-1228'' was escorted to [[Portsmouth, New Hampshire]] by {{USS|Neal A. Scott}}, arriving at 0600 hours on 17 May.{{Cite book |last=Wiberg |first=Eric |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fMq7DwAAQBAJ&dq=%22U-1228%22&pg=PT330 |title=U-Boats in New England |date=3 November 2019 |publisher=Fonthill Media |isbn=9781781557204 |language=en |chapter=Eight Surrenders: ''U-858'', ''U-1228'', ''U-805'', ''U-873'', ''U-234'', ''U-977'', ''U-889'', and ''U-530'' |access-date=14 November 2025 |via=Google Books}} ''Dione'' escorted the U-boat into Portsmouth later that day.{{Cite web |date=17 May 1945 |title=USCGC Dione (WPC-107) Escorting German Submarine U-1228, Portsmouth, New Hampshire |url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/38329755 |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=National Archives Catalog}} ''Dione'' was sent back to the Fifth Naval District in June, where she was assigned to [[Air-sea rescue|air-sea rescue duty]]. === Post-war === On 1 January 1946, jurisdiction of the Coast Guard was given back to the Department of the Treasury via [[Executive Order 9666]], signed by President [[Harry S. Truman]].{{Rp|pp=|page=21}}{{Cite web |title=Executive Order 9666 |url=https://www.trumanlibrary.gov/library/executive-orders/9666/executive-order-9666 |access-date=20 November 2025 |website=[[Harry S. Truman Library & Museum]]}} From 1945 to 1947, ''Dione'' was used by the Coast Guard for [[law enforcement]] and search and rescue. She was eventually [[Ship commissioning#Ship decommissioning|decommissioned]] on 23 July 1947, in [[Cape May, New Jersey]],[https://books.google.com/books?id=xUOyoV_c6H8C&q=%22Dione%22#v=snippet&q=%22Dione%22&f=false "Texas Towns Welcome First CG Ship There"]. ''U.S. Coast Guard Bulletin''. Vol. 7. Bureau of the Budget. May 1952. The cutter was recommissioned on 4 February 1951, in [[Curtis Bay, Baltimore|Curtis Bay, Maryland]],{{Cite journal |date=June 1952 |title=Texas! Big State with a Big Heart! |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_u-s-coast-guard-magazine_1952-06_25_8 |journal=U.S. Coast Guard Magazine |volume=25 |issue=8 |pages= |via=Internet Archive}}{{Reference page|pages=9–10|page=}} after a [[shakedown cruise]] in the [[Caribbean]]. Starting in 1952, ''Dione'' was assigned to the [[United States Coast Guard#Districts and units|Eighth Coast Guard District]] and based in [[Freeport, Texas]];{{Cite news |date=August 1951 |title=Dione is Re-Commissioned |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xUOyoV_c6H8C&q=%22Dione%22 |access-date=April 21, 2025 |work=U.S. Coast Guard Bulletin |publisher=Bureau of the Budget |pages= |via=Google Books |volume=7}}{{Reference page|pages=|page=150}} she was the first cutter to be based in the city.{{Reference page|pages=|page=185}} Reportedly, Freeport competed with the city of [[Corpus Christi, Texas|Corpus Christi]] to be the location where ''Dione'' was stationed.{{Cite news |date=18 December 1962 |title=Okay of Dione berth welcome |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/19839630/?match=1&terms=%22cutter%20Dione%22 |access-date=5 October 2025 |work=The Brazosport Facts |pages= |via=newspapers.com}}{{Reference page|pages=|page=2}} The cutter was originally scheduled to arrive on 13 March 1952 but was delayed until 19 March due to rough weather on her shakedown cruise.{{Cite news |date=13 March 1952 |title=Dione Arrival Here Delayed |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/10433108/?clipping_id=146513780&fcfToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJmcmVlLXZpZXctaWQiOjEwNDMzMTA4LCJpYXQiOjE3NTkyNTE0NDIsImV4cCI6MTc1OTMzNzg0Mn0.KReeFD_otLxdUnqnfS2fF4d-lg4HQjDMc9IH29OeI9I |access-date=30 September 2025 |work=The Freeport Facts |pages= |via=newspapers.com}}{{Reference page|pages=|page=1}} She was met with a yacht escort upon her arrival in Freeport that day. Local schools were closed so students could visit ''Dione,'' and an enlisted men's dance and officer's dinner was held.{{Reference page|pages=|page=185}}{{Reference page|pages=9–10|page=}} The day was officially proclaimed "Coast Guard Day" by the cities of Freeport, [[Velasco, Texas|Velasco]], [[Clute, Texas|Clute]], and [[Lake Jackson, Texas|Lake Jackson]].{{Reference page|pages=|page=185}}
